Data Communications

Data communication = exchanging data between TWO devices over some transmission medium (wire, fiber, air). Ch 2 Part 2, slide 2 : The transmission medium in detail Data Communications The exchange of Information between two ■ devices through a transmission medium 3 McGraw-Hill
Five components of data communication (Figure 1.1)

The 5 components: message, sender, receiver, transmission medium, protocol. The protocol sits on BOTH sides: sender and receiver must follow the same rules. “My Sister Reads The Paper”: Message, Sender, Receiver, Transmission medium, Protocol. The medium is the physical path. The protocol is the set of rules. Don’t swap them. 1.2 Networks

More throughput and less delay pull against each other: pushing more data in raises the delay. Criteria = “PRS”: Performance, Reliability, Security. MCQ 5 · failure frequency and recovery time = reliability Written Q3 · the three criteria Related question: Fill-in 3 · distributed processing Frequency of failure and recovery time after a failure measure a network’s: Network performance is evaluated by: Increasing throughput usually also increases delay. List and explain the three criteria of an effective network. 1.2 Networks A network is a set of devices (called nodes) connected by communication links. ■ Node can be host (a computer, printer, cell phone) or networking devices (routers, ■ switches, modem, etc…) Link is a communication pathway that transfer data from one device to another ■ Link can be wired or wireless ■ Type of network connections ■ Point-to-Point: dedicated link between two devices ■ Multipoint : shared link between more than two devices ■ Distributed system vs. Computer networks ■ A network must be able to meet a certain number of criteria. The most important of ■ these are: Performance ■ Depends on factors such as: ■ # of users, type of transmission medium, capabilities of Network hardware, ■ Network software efficiency Evaluated by: ■ Throughput (amount of data a user can send) ■ Delay (measured in transit time, and response time) ■ To have good performance, we need more throughput and less delay ■ (contradict each other, because when throughput increases, it means more data arrive to the network, this will increase the delay Reliability ■ Measured by: ■ Frequency of failure ■ Time it takes a link to recover from the failure ■ Security ■ Protecting data from unauthorized users, and damage, applying security policies ■ for recovery from breaches and data losses 6 McGraw-Hill

Point-to-point: a DEDICATED link between exactly two devices. Wired or wireless both count. A point-to-point connection can be wireless. Figure 1.5 Point-to-point connection 7 McGraw-Hill

Multipoint = the link’s capacity is SHARED, in space (all at once) or in time (taking turns). Data flow (direction of data flowing in the link) (Figure 1.2)

Simplex : one direction only, always (keyboard → computer, TV, radio). Half-duplex : both directions, but one at a time; each side gets the whole channel while sending (walkie-talkie). Full-duplex : both directions at the same time; the channel capacity is shared by the two directions (telephone). Half-duplex = “over” on a walkie-talkie. Full-duplex = talking over each other on the phone. Categories of topology (Figure 1.7)

Four basic ones: mesh, star, bus, ring (plus hybrids). Four topologies: “My Star Bus Rings” (Mesh, Star, Bus, Ring). Figure 1.7 Categories of topology Topology: The way in which a network is physically built or The way in which devices interconnect across the network 10 McGraw-Hill
Fully connected mesh topology (for five devices) (Figure 1.8)

Every device has a dedicated link to every other one. Links = N(N-1)/2; each device needs N-1 ports (NICs). Expensive because of all the cabling and ports: that is the answer to “why?”. N = 8 → 8 × 7 / 2 = 28 links, 7 ports per device. Ports per device is N-1, not N(N-1)/2. Fill-in 4 · mesh links = n(n-1)/2 Written Q1 · links for 8 devices Related question: Scenario 1 · offices across the world How many links are needed for a fully connected mesh of 6 devices? In a mesh of 10 devices, how many I/O ports does each device need? A mesh topology has no traffic (congestion) problems because each link is dedicated. A network has 8 devices. How many cable links does a mesh, ring, bus and star need? Figure 1.8 Fully connected mesh topology (for five devices) ▪ Dedicated point-to-point link to every other node ▪Number of links = N(N-1)/2 ▪ Advantages ▪ Dedicated links 🡺 secure, no traffic problems (no congestion) ▪ Robust: if one link fails, the network will still work ▪Easy to discover faulty links ▪ Disadvantages? ▪Difficult to install & update (too much wiring) ▪ Expensive (why?) ▪ Number of Network interface cards (NIC) or Number of I/O ports = (N-1 )per device ▪ Number of cables = Number of links 11 McGraw-Hill
Star topology (Figure 1.9)

Each device links only to the central hub/switch, so devices never talk directly. Single point of failure: the hub. One cable failing only cuts off one device. Robust ≠ fault-proof: one bad link only takes out its device, but the hub failing takes out everything. MCQ 3 · needs a central controller Scenario 2 · 20-employee office Which topology requires a central controller or hub? A 20-employee office wants every computer connected to one central device, easy to manage and to grow. Which topology, and why? Figure 1.9 Star topology ▪ Dedicated point-to-point link to a central controller only ▪ Number of links = N ▪Advantages ▪ Less expensive than mesh ▪ Easy to install ▪ Easy to add and remove devices ▪ Robust ▪Easy to discover faulty links ▪Secure but less than mesh ▪ Disadvantages? ▪ If the central device failed the whole network will not function 12 McGraw-Hill
Bus topology (Figure 1.10)

One long backbone cable; each device hangs off it on a drop line through a tap. Formulas for N devices: mesh N(N-1)/2 links and N-1 ports each · star N links · ring N links · bus 1 main cable + N drop lines. T/F 4 · one break stops the bus In a bus topology, one break in the cable can stop all transmissions on the segment. A main cable plus N drop lines describes: Figure 1.10 Bus topology ▪ Number of links = 1 Main + N droplines ▪Advantages ▪ Easy to install ▪ less cabling than mesh and hub ▪ Disadvantages? ▪ Difficult to isolate fault ▪ Difficult to add new devices ▪ A break in the bus cable stops all transmission 13 McGraw-Hill
Ring topology (Figure 1.11)

Each device links to its two neighbours; the signal goes round the ring through each device’s repeater. Not robust: one broken link or device can break the ring (unless it is a dual ring). A ring of 12 devices needs how many links? Fault isolation is easy in a ring topology. Figure 1.11 Ring topology ▪ Dedicated point-to-point link between a node and the two nodes on either side of it ▪Number of links = N ▪Advantages ▪ Easy to install ▪ less cable ▪ Easy to add or remove a device ▪ Fault isolation is easy ▪ Disadvantage? ▪Not robust 14 McGraw-Hill
A hybrid topology: a star backbone with bus or ring networks

Hybrid = a mix, e.g. a star backbone with buses or rings hanging off it. Related question: Scenario 1 · connecting offices worldwide Figure 1.9 A hybrid topology: a star backbone with three bus networks Star - Bus Star - Ring 15 McGraw-Hill

Protocol Layers and Service Models

Problem: networks are too complex to understand or build as one piece. A layer only talks to the one directly above and below it on the same machine. The boundary between two adjacent layers is called a(n): In a layered architecture, layer n-1 provides a service to layer n. Protocol Layers and Service Models Computer network architecture is complex ■ Too many components ■ How to understand its architecture? ■ How to allow developers and users to deal with this complexity? ■ Solution 🡺 ■ Computer networks functions are designed and implemented as ■ layers Layers are logical groupings of all the processes or functions ■ required for effective data exchange Layer n-1 provides some service to the layer n through a well- ■ defined interface (boundary between each two layers) Each interface defines what information, operations, and ■ services a layer must provide for the layer above it. These layers are distributed across all nodes in the network ■
Layers, protocols, and interfaces

Horizontal = protocol (layer 3 talks to the other host’s layer 3). Vertical = interface. Only layer 1 actually touches the physical medium; everything above is logical communication. Protocol ≠ interface. A protocol is between peers on different machines; an interface is between neighbours on the same machine. Rules used between the same layer on two different hosts are a: Layers, protocols, and interfaces.

Advantages of Layered Architecture

Each layer has its own unique protocols and a well-defined interface → each layer can be built independently. So different vendors can build different layers (NIC maker, OS maker, browser maker) and it still works. Give two advantages of a layered network architecture. Advantages of Layered Architecture Breaks the complicated communication process into layers of ■ simpler processes which allows easier hardware or software implementation Each layer implements distinct (different from other layers ■ and unique) set of protocols (functions), and Well-defined interface between layers n and n-1 ■ The advantage of the above two requirements: ■ The implementation of each layer can be done ■ independently of the other layers. This allows different manufacturers to supply the ■ hardware and software needed to the different layers 🡺 encourages collaboration & Competition

Layers 4–7 talk end to end; layers 1–3 talk hop by hop with every intermediate node. Peer-to-Peer Processes Peers are entities (processes, hardware devices) on two or more machines communicating at a given layer
OSI model-Basic Operation

Control info goes in a HEADER. Data link is the exception: it adds a header AND a trailer. Only the data link layer adds a trailer (for error detection). Ch 3 Part 1, slide 4 : Framing adds the header and trailer Which layer adds both a header and a trailer? The header added by the transport layer is read by the receiver’s transport layer only. OSI model-Basic Operation Peer-to-Peer communication: Each layer on a sending ■ node communicates (logically) with its peer layer on the receiving node using formatted blocks of data called Protocol Data Units (PDU) PDU = combination of data (payload) from the next higher ■ layer and the control information of the current layer (Specific requests and instructions) Control information are given in the header fields of the ■ block except for the data link (has both header and trailer) Control information is read and executed ONLY by the peer ■ layer on the receiving node

Data Encapsulation

Encapsulation: layer N-1 carries layer N’s whole PDU as its data, without looking inside. PDU (N-1) = PDU (N) + control info of N-1. Data encapsulation means that layer N-1: During encapsulation, a lower layer inspects and changes the upper layer’s header. Data Encapsulation Data encapsulation refers to the fact that layer N-1 carries in its data part the PDU of layer N without any knowledge of its content and its different parts.
Decapsulation
Decapsulation = the reverse: each layer removes its own header/trailer and hands the rest up.

Signals: data must become electromagnetic signals

Data can’t travel as-is: it must be turned into an electromagnetic signal (voltage on copper, light in fiber, radio in air). To be transmitted, data must be transformed to electromagnetic signals. A Transmission System

Analog and Digital

Analog/digital is about the VALUES; periodic/aperiodic is about the PATTERN over time. They are separate classifications. A signal that can have an infinite number of values in a range is: A periodic signal repeats its pattern over identical periods called cycles. A medium passes some frequencies, blocks others and weakens others, so the output never equals the input exactly. Signal corruption ▪ No transmission medium can pass all the signal frequencies safely ▪A medium may ▪ Pass some frequencies ▪ Block others ▪ Weaken others
Transmission Impairments

Three impairments: attenuation, distortion, noise. “ADN”: Attenuation (weaker), Distortion (reshaped), Noise (extra signal). Which is NOT a transmission impairment? Transmission Impairments Impairments: Factors that make the received signal different from the transmitted one
Attenuation

Attenuation = LOSS OF ENERGY (the wire heats up). Worse with distance and with higher frequency. Fix: amplifiers for analog, repeaters for digital (they regenerate a clean copy). Amplifiers boost noise too; repeaters regenerate the original bits. Noise

Framing

Framing = packing bits into frames so the receiver knows where each one starts and ends (like envelopes). The destination address says where it goes; the sender address lets the receiver acknowledge it. Framing • The data-link layer needs to pack bits into frames, so that each frame is distinguishable from another. • Our postal system practices a type of framing. The simple act of inserting a letter into an envelope separates one piece of information from another; the envelope serves as the 0. • Framing in the data-link layer separates a message from one source to a destination by adding a sender address and a destination address. • The destination address defines where the packet is to go; the sender address helps the recipient acknowledge the receipt.
